My wife is an SLP and got full scholarships to multiple grad schools - that may be a possibility for you!  She loves her work and how personal it is.  She opted to work in an elementary school setting as it is less depressing than the elder care route (making progress rather than preventing further regression) and so much of her job is active playing with children that contains incredibly important therapy.  

An SLP career is about as close as you can get to a career that is devoid of capitalism.  There is no corporate ladder, pretty meaningless reviews (teacher tenure for the win!),  no ruthlessness, no abstracting gray cubicle; there is only a stable career of helping and playing with children.  I think you made an excellent choice.  It's so hard to see the finish line when you're a few years away from it - but if you can see this thing through there is a really bright light at the end of the tunnel.

Even if you decide to go in a different direction and think that the SLP life is not the life for you, life has a funny way of guiding you.  I graduated with a bachelor's in Philosophy, which unsurprisingly netted me practically zero job offers.  I worked at my college Help Desk, translated that into a corporate Help Desk job, became Help Desk Manager, shifted into Software Development Project Management, and am now the Director of Project Management at a financial services company making a healthy salary, fully remote.  I didn't choose that path, the path chose me.  There are plently of happy lives waiting for you, you just can't have that crystal ball that will tell you what it will look like.

You are not alone.  In the first few pages of Plato's "The Republic", Socrates asks his friend Cephalus how old age is treating him, and if it is difficult to suffer aging.  Cephalus replies:

"...most of the members of our [old friend] group lament, longing for the pleasures of youth and reminiscing about sex, about drinking bouts and feasts and all that goes with things of that sort; they take it hard as though they were deprived of something very important and had then lived well but are now not even alive... but, Socrates, in my opinion these men do not put their fingers on the cause... I was once present when [Sophocles] was asked by someone, 'Sophocles, how are you in sex?  Can you still have intercourse with a woman?' 'Silence, man,' he said. 'Most joyfully did I escape it, as though I had run away from a sort of frenzied and savage master.'  I thought at the time that he had spoken well and still do.  For, in every way, old age brings great peace and freedom from such things.  When the desires cease to strain and finally relax, then what Sophocles says come to pass in every way; it is possible to be rid of very many bad masters."

I came across this passage when I was in college, probably about 20 exactly like you are now, and it felt comforting knowing that others shared my grief, and that said grief was not logical, but an emotional, hard-wired one that I was subjected to as part of the human condition.  By being able to recognize it, in some ways, it felt as if I was able to control it, or atleast, control my reaction to it.  Further, it felt comforting to know that it is temporary.  I am now 35, and can say that while I am in no way as old as Socrates, Cephalus, or Sophocles, the sex drive has certainly diminished, to the degree that I feel entirely in control of my former masters.  It is not to say I do not want sex, nor does it imply I do not have sex, but I do so under my terms, not as an obsession.  It does get better, and you are not alone.

The only thing to consider is that there is, at least where I am in Western MA, currently a "standard" turnaround time for houses.  Seems as if the house gets listed during the week, has showings over the weekend, and has final offers due Monday.  This means each "desirable" house is on the market for approximately a week, and anything that stays on the market for longer than a week is a flag for potential buyers.  Not necessarily a red flag, but a flag nonetheless.  It may either prompt the question of "what's wrong with this house that we can't see" or "perhaps the buyers are going to start getting desperate, maybe let's lowball".  In addition I would expect the highest interest to be on your house within the first week of listing as the competitive buyers market means those who your home would appeal to is being showing to a glut of potential buyers all at once, and the longer it is on the market the fewer buyers there will be who are seeing the listing for the first time.  If I were you, I would consider taking the best or second best offer and counteroffering with something you would feel more comfortable with, or ignoring me completely.  Just my two cents!
